newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EMU outlook clouded by gold row, French poll.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EMU outlook clouded by gold row, French poll.

text.p: The prospects for Europe's monetary union were dented on Friday by an escalating row between Bonn and the German central bank, a cliff-hanger French election and Italy's fragile economy slithering into recession.

A war of words erupted between the German government and the fiercely independent Bundesbank over Bonn's plan to revalue gold reserves -- decried by many as a desperate ploy to fudge its accounts and squeeze into economic and monetary union (EMU).

The plan, designed to bolster shaky government finances, has angered the opposition, public opinion and some of Germany's EU partners, including those that Germany has accused of resorting to creative accounting to try to muscle into the EMU starting line-up.
Now Germany stands charged with the same offence.

However, Germany's recent insistence that Italy's economy was too weak to justify an early EMU berth gained fresh credence from a surprise fall in Italian first quarter gross domestic product (GDP), prompting talk of a recession and calls for an interest rate cut.
In Rome, the cabinet unveiled three-year economic targets and insisted that Italy would still make it into the first wave of a single currency when it is launched in 1999.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi said the government planned to cut the 1998 budget deficit by 25 trillion lire ($15 billion) to get a deficit to GDP ratio of 2.8 percent, below the three percent target required for membership of the single currency.
Earlier, Spain's budget secretary Jose Barea stoked EMU doubts by saying that Italy's high debts and budget deficit made it unlikely that Rome could make the euro's starting line-up.

Those doubting that a strong euro could start on schedule in 19 months time were also watching the final stages of campaigning for Sunday's crucial runoff election in France, where the Socialists scented victory in their bid for control of parliament.
Financial markets believe the French Left, if it wins, will press for a broad monetary union with more countries in from the start, including Italy and Spain.
Economists, weighing the chances of a weak EMU on time versus a delay -- both of which would damage the ambitious project's credibility -- see a broader EMU watering down the planned euro currency.
Markets, already nervous over the EMU implications of the German squabble and the French election, were watching for signs of central banks stepping in to halt any fall in their currencies.
German share dealers said the clash between Finance Minister Theo Waigel and the Bundesbank had hit market sentiment and helped drag the blue chip DAX index down by 2.44 percent.
Rumours continued to sweep the markets that the row could force either Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer or Waigel to resign.

The bank, a leading crusader for a strong euro, has condemned the revaluation of Germany's reserves as damaging to the euro's credibility and an affront to the bank's independence from meddling politicians.

In a newspaper interview to be published on Saturday, Waigel dismissed calls for his head and said Bonn would press on with its plan to revalue bank assets to repay debt and help Bonn qualify for the single currency.

Leaders from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and his junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats, stressed that the Bundesbank supported the basic plan to revalue the reserves and only opposed the timing.
Despite an eagerness to seek a compromise solution, they said there was nothing the Bundesbank could do to prevent legislation to revalue reserves this year.
However, cracks appeared in Kohl's slim parliamentary majority, with CDU deputy Juergen Augustinowitz saying he would not vote for legislation against the Bundesbank's will.
Further pressure came from a group representing Germany's largest private banks which said the gold plan was problematic, and warned that the rift could damage Germany's reputation.
Juergen Pfister, economist at Commerzbank, said Waigel could not afford to scrap his plan and that the Bundesbank would have to back down, but may force "cosmetic concessions."
